Only one LH ocean carrier exists as 2 of 2025, the Suiso Frontier, which completed its first voyage in 2022 from Kobe, Japan, to Victoria, Australia. The vessel was constructed as part of the Hydrogen Energy Supply Chain pilot project and can carry roughly 75 metric tons of LH per trip (Hydrogen Council 2022; 2 Snyder 2022). As a comparison, a single large ammonia ocean carriers can hold up to 50,000 metric tons (Atchison 2024). Larger LH carrier vessels are under development, particularly in 2 South Korea, with the largest future ocean carriers expected to hold up to about 104 metric tons (Snyder 2022; Ng 2025). Also of note, CB&I has partnered with Shell, GenH2, and the University of Houston to create a first-of-its-kind liquid hydrogen storage tank (up to about 7,000 metric tons). The tank is designed specifically for international trade applications and uses a novel non-vacuum design. This concept could provide considerable cost advantage over conventional vacuum-insulated tanks (GenH2 2025). For international hydrogen trade via ocean carriers, private industry has focused more on hydrogen carriers, such as ammonia or methanol, as the transport medium over LH (BNEF 2 2024). The reasoning for this is threefold. First, carriers such as ammonia have a higher density of hydrogen when transported than LH (107 kg H /m3 for ammonia versus 71 kg H /m3 for 2 2 2 LH ), meaning more hydrogen can be transported on a single trip, reducing transport costs. 2 Second, hydrogen carriers are transported near or at ambient temperature and pressure, thus requiring less equipment and energy input to keep the commodity from changing phase during transport. This is compared to liquid hydrogen, which must be maintained below −253°C (20 K) to avoid boil-off. Third, methanol and ammonia transport by ocean is much more established, with port infrastructure already in place for sending and/or receiving ammonia in many 54 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. countries. Given the difference in fluid properties between LH and more commonly traded 2 commodities (e.g., LNG, anhydrous ammonia, methanol, petroleum), it is unlikely that port infrastructure in place (e.g., storage, liquefiers, compressors, commodity transfer equipment) will be fully compatible without major retrofits or replacements (Thyssenkrupp 2025). Another potential benefit of transporting hydrogen in the form of ammonia or methanol is that transport infrastructure, such as pipelines, trucks, and railcars, is established and highly commercialized (Cao et al. 2025). However, a downside to transporting hydrogen in the form of a carrier, especially if for aircraft operating on liquid hydrogen, is that once the carrier reaches either the marine port or airport, it must be converted back into pure hydrogen and liquefied. The cost and space footprint of these additional steps are important for an airport to consider when selecting a supplier.
